strengths: The paper addresses a real evaluation gap in audio-text retrieval: standard caption-style benchmarks do not reflect many user query forms, especially command-like and exclusionary queries. The UIQ taxonomy is well motivated and clearly connected to prior work on query variation and negation in retrieval.

The empirical story is mostly careful and appropriately nuanced. The authors do not overclaim state-of-the-art text-to-audio retrieval; they show OEA is competitive with M2D-CLAP while being stronger in text-to-text retrieval and hard-negative discrimination.

The hard negative evaluation is a useful contribution. Metrics such as HNSR, TFR, and rank separation capture behavior that ordinary R@k misses, and the results show a consistent advantage for OEA on exclusion-aware retrieval.
The paper includes useful leakage analysis for WavCaps versus AudioCaps/Clotho and evaluates on MECAT as a cleaner benchmark, which strengthens the methodological discussion.
Implementation details are reasonably complete: backbone choices, LoRA configuration, projection heads, loss, datasets, training stages, and efficiency measurements are described.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is heavily synthetic. UIQs are generated from captions using GPT-5.1 with vocabulary grounding and length constraints, so the evaluation may test robustness to controlled prompt transformations more than real user behavior. The human validation covers only 75 audio clips and evaluates query validity, not whether the query distribution matches actual search logs.

The claimed release is problematic in the manuscript: the footnote and conclusion visibly say resources are available at a blank location. The full UIQ datasets are also described as released upon publication, which weakens current reproducibility.

The main model contribution is somewhat incremental: OEA mainly adapts existing multimodal LLM backbones with LoRA and projection heads under a standard contrastive objective. The strongest gains arise in T2T retrieval, where large LLM text encoders have an expected advantage over CLAP text encoders, rather than in the central T2A task.

The central T2A results are mixed. M2D-CLAP remains best on AudioCaps and best on several UIQ averages, while OEA gains are concentrated in imperative queries and hard-negative metrics. This supports a sound Findings-level contribution but not a strong main-conference case.

The hard-negative gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms: HNSR@10 improves by 4.3 points over M2D-CLAP and remains low overall. More analysis of failure cases and statistical significance would make the discrimination claims more convincing.

Some comparisons may be affected by differing training data and contamination histories of pretrained baselines. The paper discusses leakage and blocklists for OEA, but it is less clear how fully comparable all pretrained CLAP baselines are under the same contamination controls.

strengths: The paper addresses a real evaluation gap in audio-text retrieval: caption-style benchmarks do not fully reflect question, command, keyword, paraphrase, and exclusion-style user queries. The UIQ taxonomy and hard-negative discrimination framing are relevant to NLP/CL retrieval evaluation.

The experimental comparison is reasonably broad, covering multiple CLAP baselines, three OEA backbones, three evaluation datasets, and both standard retrieval and proposed negative-query metrics. Including vanilla multimodal LLM baselines helps show that retrieval-specific adaptation is necessary.

The paper is unusually careful about dataset contamination in audio retrieval. The AudioCaps/Clotho overlap analysis with WavCaps is a useful contribution and strengthens the motivation for including MECAT as a cleaner benchmark.

The proposed HNSR/TFR-style metrics capture a limitation of ordinary R@k for exclusionary queries: retrieving the target while also suppressing a confusable hard negative. This is a sensible and practically meaningful evaluation direction.

The implementation description includes core architectural and training details such as frozen backbones, LoRA configuration, projection heads, InfoNCE objective, training data stages, and inference cost measurements.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated relative to the results. OEA is not clearly superior for the primary text-to-audio task: M2D-CLAP is best on AudioCaps and best on average UIQ, while OEA’s strongest gains are in text-to-text retrieval and a subset of imperative/negative-query metrics. The paper’s framing often reads stronger than the evidence supports.

The T2T evaluation is not sufficiently justified as evidence for audio-text retrieval. It appears to rely on caption-based retrieval, but the paper does not clearly establish whether realistic automatically generated captions are used at indexing time or whether gold/reference captions leak semantic information. This makes the large T2T gains less decisive for the stated task.

The UIQ benchmark is mostly synthetically generated using a single proprietary LLM, with only 75 audio clips/675 ratings for human validation. This is too small to strongly support claims about real-world search behavior, especially for negative and exclusionary queries, which have the lowest human validity scores and highest variance.

The paper motivates UIQs through real user behavior, but it does not evaluate on real query logs or human-authored search queries. The Freesound length analysis is discussed, yet the generated queries are intentionally constrained around original caption lengths, so the benchmark may still be closer to caption transformation than authentic user intent.

The negative-query setup may bake in artifacts: queries are generated from both target and hard-negative captions, and hard negatives are mined partly with embedding models. Although human verification is mentioned, the scale, criteria, and inter-annotator reliability of this verification are not reported.

The reported hard-negative improvements are modest in absolute terms. For example, HNSR@10 improves from 30.3 to 34.6, while standard negative-query R@5/R@10 remains better for M2D-CLAP. The paper should temper claims of substantially superior semantic understanding or provide stronger statistical evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time. The paper says datasets/checkpoints/demo will be released, and full UIQ datasets only upon publication, but reviewers cannot verify generation outputs, filtering, hard-negative pairs, or model checkpoints. Reliance on proprietary GPT-5.1 and Claude Opus 4.5 also limits exact reproduction.

Important experimental details are missing or underdeveloped: random seeds, variance across runs, significance tests, exact blocklist application after leakage detection, baseline fine-tuning/evaluation parity, and the size/composition of final negative-query sets per dataset.

The writing is generally understandable but sometimes promotional. Terms such as “dominant,” “substantially superior,” and “semantic understanding” are used where the evidence supports a narrower conclusion: competitive T2A performance with some advantages on specific synthetic query types and metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses a real evaluation gap in audio-text retrieval: standard caption-style benchmarks do not reflect many user query formulations. The UIQ taxonomy is well motivated and useful, especially the inclusion of imperative, keyphrase, paraphrase, and exclusionary queries.

The experimental setup is broad and comparatively strong: the paper evaluates multiple OEA backbones, several CLAP baselines including M2D-CLAP, and three datasets. The explicit data-leakage analysis for WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps and Clotho is a particularly valuable contribution and improves confidence in the reported comparisons.

The proposed OEA architecture is simple, reproducible in principle, and sensible: frozen multimodal LLM backbones with LoRA adapters and modality-specific projection heads. The paper provides key training details, hyperparameters, prompts, validation protocol, and efficiency measurements.

The results support a nuanced claim rather than a blanket win: OEA is competitive but not clearly superior for standard T2A retrieval, while showing stronger text-to-text retrieval and better hard-negative discrimination. This distinction is useful for practitioners choosing between CLAP-style models and LLM-based encoders.

The hard-negative discrimination metrics are a valuable addition because standard R@k can miss whether models suppress acoustically similar distractors. The negative-query analysis is one of the more interesting parts of the paper.
weaknesses: The central UIQ benchmark is synthetic, generated by a single LLM under controlled constraints. Human validation covers only 75 samples and asks whether queries make sense relative to captions, which is weaker than validating whether they reflect real user search behavior or preserve the intended audio semantics at scale.

The gains that most distinguish OEA are somewhat narrow. Standard T2A and average UIQ performance are often led by M2D-CLAP, and OEA’s hard-negative gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms, e.g. +4.3 points HNSR@10. The paper sometimes phrases these results more strongly than the evidence warrants.

The T2T results are strong, but they evaluate caption-to-caption retrieval rather than direct audio retrieval. Their practical relevance depends on the availability and quality of an upstream audio captioning system, whose errors and latency are not evaluated end to end.

The hard-negative construction pipeline depends on MGA-CLAP and BGE filtering before human verification, which may shape the benchmark toward particular notions of acoustic and semantic confusability. More detail on the size and rigor of human verification would strengthen confidence.

Reproducibility is good in intent but not fully established from the manuscript alone: it claims release of checkpoints, demo, and UIQ datasets, but some full datasets are described as available only upon publication, and the visible manuscript appears to omit or anonymize the actual release URL.

The paper would benefit from stronger statistical analysis or uncertainty estimates. Many comparisons are close, and significance testing or bootstrap confidence intervals would help distinguish robust findings from benchmark variance.

strengths: The paper targets a real evaluation gap in audio-text retrieval: standard caption-style benchmarks do not reflect many user query formulations. The UIQ taxonomy and exclusionary-query evaluation are relevant to NLP/CL retrieval and make the evaluation story broader than another CLAP leaderboard comparison.

The experimental coverage is fairly broad: multiple datasets, several CLAP baselines including M2D-CLAP, three multimodal-LLM backbones, vanilla LALM controls, T2A/T2T settings, and efficiency measurements.
The authors are unusually explicit about data contamination between WavCaps and AudioCaps/Clotho, and the inclusion of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark strengthens the evidence for generalization.

The hard-negative discrimination metrics are well motivated. HNSR and related metrics expose behavior that standard R@k can hide, and the paper usefully distinguishes standard retrieval quality from suppression of acoustically similar distractors.

The mechanism ablations in Appendix O are a strong point: they temper the initial “LLM understands negation” interpretation and show that OEA’s advantage is mainly audio-space separation plus general order sensitivity, rather than a unique text-side negation mechanism.
weaknesses: The central empirical gains are more modest than the framing sometimes suggests. M2D-CLAP remains best on mean T2A and average UIQ, while OEA’s clearest advantages are T2T and hard-negative discrimination. This supports a sound contribution, but not a uniformly superior retrieval model.

The UIQ benchmark is entirely synthetic and only lightly human-validated: 75 of 13,053 queries are rated. The queries are also constrained to reuse caption vocabulary and length, which weakens the claim that they reflect real-world user behavior, especially given cited evidence that real audio-search queries are often very short.

The T2T result is useful but somewhat expected because OEA uses a billion-parameter LLM backbone for text-text matching while CLAP baselines use smaller text encoders. It is also not a direct audio retrieval setting unless a separate captioning system is assumed, whose errors and costs are not evaluated end-to-end.

The hard-negative benchmark depends on MGA-CLAP and BGE for mining, with only sampled human threshold calibration rather than per-pair validation. This may bias the definition of “hard” and may omit important perceptual confusions outside the miner’s embedding space.

Reproducibility is partly incomplete from the manuscript alone. Prompts, main hyperparameters, and generation settings are provided, but full training schedules, random seeds, exact blocklists, checkpoint availability, and statistical uncertainty for main retrieval results are not sufficiently detailed. Dependence on proprietary GPT/Claude models for benchmark generation/validation also complicates exact reproduction.

The paper would benefit from stronger statistical reporting. Many differences are small, especially across UIQ/T2A tables, but confidence intervals or significance tests are mostly absent outside the mechanism ablations.

The architecture contribution is incremental: frozen native-audio multimodal LLMs with LoRA adapters, projection heads, mean pooling, and contrastive training. The strongest contribution is the evaluation framework rather than a clearly novel modeling method.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant evaluation gap: audio-text retrieval benchmarks over-rely on caption-style queries, while real search often uses commands, keywords, paraphrases, and exclusions.
The manuscript is unusually explicit about dataset contamination between WavCaps, AudioCaps, and Clotho, and the inclusion of MECAT as a leakage-conscious benchmark is valuable.
The experiments cover several strong CLAP baselines, multiple OEA backbones, standard T2A/T2T retrieval, UIQ variants, efficiency, and several mechanism ablations.
The appendix ablations are candid and useful: they show that the hard-negative gains are mainly due to audio-space separation rather than a unique LLM-based understanding of negation.
weaknesses: The central framing is overstated. OEA does not clearly improve the main text-to-audio retrieval task: M2D-CLAP remains best on the mean T2A results, and OEA’s gains are mostly in T2T retrieval or narrow hard-negative metrics.

The UIQ benchmark is synthetic and weakly validated. Only 75 of 13,053 generated queries are human-rated, the queries are constrained to reuse caption vocabulary and similar lengths, and the paper does not compare the resulting distribution to real audio-search logs. This limits the claim that UIQ reflects real user intent.

The negative-query evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate exclusion or negation understanding. The paper’s own ablations show that adding the exclusion clause hurts every model and that OEA’s advantage comes chiefly from pre-existing target/hard-negative audio separation.

The hard-negative benchmark may be biased by its construction. Pairs are mined with MGA-CLAP and BGE, and human validation calibrates thresholds only on samples rather than auditing mined pairs. This makes the metric sensitive to the mining pipeline and not necessarily to robust semantic exclusion.
Some metrics and summaries are difficult to interpret. Table 4 mixes R@5 for positive UIQ types with HNSR@10 for exclusionary queries in a single Avg UIQ, combining non-equivalent quantities.

The T2T contribution is not well connected to practical audio retrieval. It appears to evaluate text-query to text-caption matching, but a deployed caption-based retrieval system would depend on generated captions and their errors; the paper does not fully evaluate that pipeline.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. It gives high-level training details and prompts, but important implementation choices, exact blocklists, mined-pair datasets, validation samples, and baseline evaluation parity would need released artifacts to verify the claims.

The paper repeatedly uses strong language such as 'dominant' and 'superior semantic understanding' despite modest or mixed gains, high computational cost, and evidence that the main advantage is not the claimed text-side reasoning mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation gap in audio-text retrieval: current benchmarks overemphasize caption-style queries, while real search includes questions, commands, keywords, paraphrases, and exclusions. The UIQ framing is well motivated and relevant to NLP/CL retrieval.

The empirical comparison is broad, covering AudioCaps, Clotho, and MECAT, multiple CLAP baselines, vanilla audio LLMs, and several OEA backbones. The inclusion of MECAT and explicit leakage analysis for WavCaps/AudioCaps/Clotho is a notable strength.

The claims are mostly calibrated: OEA is not presented as uniformly better on standard text-to-audio retrieval, but as competitive there and stronger for text-to-text retrieval and hard-negative discrimination.

The hard-negative evaluation is thoughtful. HNSR, TFR, and rank-gap metrics capture behavior that standard R@k misses, and the mechanism ablations in Appendix O substantially improve the soundness of the discrimination claim.
Reproducibility is helped by detailed training settings, UIQ generation prompts, metric definitions, reported dataset sizes, and a stated release of benchmarks, code, and checkpoints.
weaknesses: The main architectural novelty is moderate: OEA is largely an adaptation of existing native-audio multimodal LLM backbones with LoRA and projection heads for contrastive retrieval. The strongest contribution may be the evaluation suite rather than the model itself.

The UIQ benchmark is synthetic and only lightly human-validated: 75 samples out of 13,053 queries were rated. This supports plausibility but not strong coverage guarantees, especially for negative queries, which have the lowest human validity score.
The use of proprietary or not-easily-reproducible generators/evaluators such as GPT-5.1 and Claude Opus 4.5 weakens benchmark reproducibility and may make future regeneration or auditing difficult.

The central performance story is mixed. M2D-CLAP remains best on average UIQ and standard T2A in several settings, while OEA’s strongest gains are in T2T retrieval and hard-negative discrimination. T2T retrieval is useful, but it assumes an audio-captioning pipeline and is not the same problem as direct audio retrieval.

The hard-negative set depends on MGA-CLAP for acoustic candidate mining. The authors acknowledge this and add calibration, but the benchmark may still emphasize confusion types visible to that model rather than a model-independent notion of perceptual confusability.

Efficiency is a practical concern: OEA is much heavier than CLAP baselines in memory and audio encoding latency. The offline-indexing argument helps but does not fully remove deployment cost concerns.

Some comparisons may be affected by differences in pretraining exposure and contamination across released baselines, even though the authors analyze and mitigate leakage for their own training setup. This complicates direct interpretation of absolute benchmark numbers.
